etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smoke, from Old English smoca (“smoke”), probably a derivative of the verb (see below). Related to Dutch smook (“smoke”), Middle Low German smôk (“smoke”), dialectal German Schmauch (“smoke”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The visible vapor/vapour, gases, and fine particles given off by burning or smoldering material.

quote.citation: 1952 October, C. A. Johns, “One Hundred Years at Kings Cross—1”, in Railway Magazine, page 657:
quote.text: If those were the days, however, when steam was triumphant, they were also the days of smoke. Nowhere was this so apparent as at "Kings Cross (Suburban)" where, one after another, the Great Northern tank engines thumped their way up the incline and emerged from the tunnel, in clouds of steam and smoke, to pound their way up the last few hundred feet of gradient alongside the platform.

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “Unspontaneous combustion”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 29:
quote.text: Since the mid-1980s, when Indonesia first began to clear its bountiful forests on an industrial scale in favour of lucrative palm-oil plantations, “haze” has become an almost annual occurrence in South-East Asia. The cheapest way to clear logged woodland is to burn it, producing an acrid cloud of foul white smoke that, carried by the wind, can cover hundreds, or even thousands, of square miles.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, countable) A cigarette.

quote.citation: 2019, Idles, "Never Fight a Man With a Perm", Joy as an Act of Resistance.
quote.text: I said I've got a penchant for smokes and kicking douches in the mouth / Sadly for you my last cigarette's gone out

definitions.definition: (colloquial, uncountable) Anything to smoke (e.g. cigarettes, marijuana, etc.)

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Noveria:
quote.text: ERCS Guard: Got a smoke? We're all out.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, countable, never plural) An instance of smoking a cigarette, cigar, etc.; the duration of this act.

quote.citation: 1884 December 10, Mark Twain [pseudonym; Samuel Langhorne Clemens], chapter VII, in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn: (Tom Sawyer’s Comrade) […], London: Chatto & Windus, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I lit a pipe and had a good long smoke, and went on watching.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, figuratively) A fleeting illusion; something insubstantial, evanescent, unreal, transitory, or without result.

quote.citation: 1974, John le Carré, chapter 6, in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy‎[1], New York: Knopf, page 44:
quote.text: I fed her a lot of smoke about a sheep station outside Adelaide and a big property in the high street with a glass front and ‘Thomas’ in lights. She didn’t believe me.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, figuratively) Something used to obscure or conceal; an obscuring condition; see also smoke and mirrors.
(uncountable) A light grey color tinted with blue.
(uncountable, slang) Bother; problems; hassle.

(military, uncountable) A particulate of solid or liquid particles dispersed into the air on the battlefield to degrade enemy ground or for aerial observation. Smoke has many uses--screening smoke, signaling smoke, smoke curtain, smoke haze, and smoke deception. Thus it is an artificial aerosol.
(baseball, slang) A fastball.
(countable) A distinct column of smoke, such as indicating a burning area or fire.

quote.citation: 1860, Randolph Barnes Marcy, The Prairie and Overland Traveller, page 203:
quote.text: Should the commander of one column desire to communicate with the other, he raises three smokes simultaneously, which, if seen by the other party, should be responded to in the same manner.

quote.citation: 1923, California Historical Society Quarterly, volume 2, page 152:
quote.text: […]  and we could not discern any settlement or any people, but we did see two smokes up-river in some thick groves of oak and cork and willows and other high trees, of a good thickness, resembling ash trees.

quote.citation: 1941 January, C. Hamilton Ellis, “The Scottish Station”, in Railway Magazine, page 1:
quote.text: In the evening haze, even the Calton Gaol took on something of the savage grandeur of a Doré drawing, and this was by no means spoilt by the rising smokes of North British engines in the ravine below.

quote.citation: 1957, Sylva: The Lands and Forests Review, volumes 13-14, page 43:
quote.text: During the night, a severe lightning storm passed over this area and in the morning the towerman reported two smokes separated by about two miles distance.

quote.citation: 2021 May 15, “Guadalupe Mountains National Park Temporarily Closes Backcountry Campsites due to Dog Fire”, in Guadalupe Mountains National Park News Releases‎[2]:
quote.text: The aerial reconnaissance did see active flame on heavy fuels (logs) and fine fuels (duff/understory), and several smokes.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smoken, from Old English smocian (“to smoke, emit smoke; fumigate”), from Proto-West Germanic *smokōn, from Proto-Germanic *smukōną (“to smoke”), ablaut derivative of Proto-Germanic *smaukaną (“to smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewg- (“to smoke”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian smookje (“to smoke”), West Frisian smoke (“to smoke”), Dutch smoken (“to smoke”), Low German smöken (“to smoke”), German Low German smoken (“to smoke”). Related also to Old English smēocan (“to smoke, emit smoke; fumigate”), Bavarian schmuckelen (“to smell bad, reek”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To inhale and exhale the smoke from a burning cigarette, cigar, pipe, etc.
(intransitive) To inhale and exhale tobacco smoke.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 2:
quote.text: He used to drop into my chambers once in a while to smoke, and was first-rate company. When I gave a dinner there was generally a cover laid for him. I liked the man for his own sake, and even had he promised to turn out a celebrity it would have had no weight with me.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: To Edward  […]  he was terrible, nerve-inflaming, poisonously asphyxiating. He sat rocking himself in the late Mr. Churchill's swing chair, smoking and twaddling.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Of a fire in a fireplace: to emit smoke outward instead of up the chimney, owing to imperfect draught.
(intransitive) To give off smoke.

quote.citation: 1645, John Milton, L'Allegro:
quote.text: Hard by a cottage chimney smokes.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To preserve or prepare (food) for consumption by treating with smoke.
(transitive) To dry or medicate by smoke.

quote.citation: 2019, Thomas D. Seeley, The Lives of Bees: The Untold Story of the Honey Bee in the Wild, page 64:
quote.text: After opening one of the hives from the back, he smoked the bees to calm them and to drive the queen toward the front of the hive.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To fill or scent with smoke; hence, to fill with incense; to perfume.
(transitive, obsolete) To make unclear or blurry.

quote.citation: 1820, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Oedipus Tyrannus; Or, Swellfoot The Tyrant: A Tragedy in Two Acts:
quote.text: Smoke your bits of glass,Ye loyal Swine, or her transfigurationWill blind your wondering eyes.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, slang, chiefly as present participle) To perform (e.g. music) energetically or skillfully.
(slang) To beat someone at something.
